edges.label: Marcel was the 509th intelligence officer who recovered the debris
edges.note: Marcel and Cavitt were assigned by RAAF to retrieve the material from the Foster Ranch after Brazel reported it to Sheriff Wilcox on 6 July 1947.

edges.label: Mogul is the Air Force's 1994 identification of the debris
edges.note: The 1994 USAF report attributed the debris to Project Mogul Flight No. 4, launched 4 June 1947 from Alamogordo, and acknowledged that the weather balloon account had been a cover story.

edges.label: Ramey retracted the RAAF statement the same day at Fort Worth
edges.note: Brig. Gen. Roger M. Ramey, commanding Eighth Air Force, presented the debris as a weather balloon and radar target with weather officer Irving Newton. The Air Force conceded in 1994 that this was a cover story.

b.label: Roswell, New Mexico and the Foster Ranch, Lincoln County

edges.label: The 1947 recovery was executed by Roswell Army Air Field
edges.note: Maj. Jesse Marcel of the 509th Bomb Group intelligence office and Capt. Sheridan Cavitt of the Counter Intelligence Corps were dispatched from RAAF to the Foster Ranch. Attested by the 1947 press record and the Air Force's own reports.

b.label: White Sands Missile Range, New Mexico

edges.label: Roswell sits inside the 1947 New Mexico nuclear and rocketry complex
edges.note: The Foster Ranch debris field, White Sands Proving Ground, the Alamogordo Mogul launch site, Los Alamos, Sandia and Kirtland all lie within a few hundred miles. Reasoning: geographic proximity is the reason a materiel recovery there fell inside multiple classified security envelopes at once.

edges.label: Haut issued the 8 July 1947 'flying disc' press release
edges.note: 1st Lt. Walter Haut, RAAF public information officer, issued the release stating the 509th's intelligence office had gained possession of a disc.
